The immune system remembers past pathogens for faster future response.
T cells attacking infected host cells directly.

interactive_questions.title: Antibody Specificity
interactive_questions.prompt: Match antibodies to their specific antigens! Select an antibody, then click matching antigens.
interactive_questions.question: Match 5 antigens to continue.
interactive_questions.explanation: Antibodies have specific binding sites that only recognize antigens with complementary shapes - this is called specificity. Each antibody type can only bind to one antigen type.

theory.title: Antibody Specificity
theory.content:
Antibodies (Immunoglobulins) are Y-shaped proteins produced by B cells. The tips of the 'Y' are variable regions that form a specific lock-and-key fit with a unique part of a pathogen called an Antigen.

This specificity allows the immune system to target a specific virus (like flu) without accidentally attacking healthy cells or other beneficial bacteria.
theory.analogy: Antibodies are like police handcuffs that are custom-made to fit only one specific criminal's wrists. They won't work on anyone else.
theory.application: Monoclonal antibody therapy uses lab-made antibodies designed to target specific cancer cells or autoimmune markers, acting like guided missiles for treatment.

interactive_questions.title: Cellular Immunity
interactive_questions.prompt: Different immune cells have specialized roles.
interactive_questions.question: Which immune cell directly kills virus-infected cells?
interactive_questions.explanation: Cytotoxic T cells (CD8+ T cells) directly kill infected cells by recognizing viral antigens on cell surfaces and inducing apoptosis (cell death).

theory.title: T Cell Function
theory.content: Cytotoxic T Cells are the assassins of the immune system. They scan body cells for signs of infection (viral antigens presented on the surface). If detected, they release toxic granules that force the infected cell to self-destruct.
theory.analogy: If B cells are the artillery firing missiles (antibodies) from a distance, Cytotoxic T cells are the special ops soldiers engaging in close-quarters combat to neutralize targets.
theory.application: In organ transplants, these T cells often recognize the new organ as 'foreign' and attack it, causing rejection. Patients take immunosuppressants to calm these T cells down.

critical_concepts.elaboration: Slow, lower magnitude response upon first exposure to an antigen.
Rapid, massive response upon re-exposure due to memory B cells.
The rapid multiplication of a specific B or T cell after it encounters its matching antigen.

interactive_questions.title: Antibody Titer Simulation
interactive_questions.prompt: Investigate the difference between first and second exposure to a pathogen.
interactive_questions.question: Inject Antigen A twice. Compare the second peak to the first.
options: Second peak is slower and smaller
Second peak is faster and larger
interactive_questions.answer: Second peak is faster and larger
interactive_questions.explanation: The secondary immune response is characterized by a shorter lag phase, a steeper rise in antibody levels, and a much higher peak titer due to the activation of Memory B cells.

theory.title: Immunological Memory
theory.content:
Primary Response: When the body first sees a pathogen, it takes days to select and clone the right B cells. IgM antibodies are produced first, followed by IgG.

Secondary Response: Memory B cells from the first encounter persist. Upon re-exposure, they differentiate into plasma cells almost instantly, producing massive amounts of high-affinity IgG antibodies.
theory.analogy: The first time you drive to a new location, you drive slowly and check the map often (Primary Response). The second time, you remember the route and drive there quickly and confidently without stopping (Secondary Response).
theory.application: Booster shots exploit this mechanism. They mimic a 're-exposure', forcing the body to expand its population of memory cells and keep antibody levels high for long-term protection.

interactive_questions.title: Clonal Selection
interactive_questions.prompt: The body has millions of B cells, but only one matches the invader. Find it to start the defense.
interactive_questions.question: What happens immediately after the correct B cell is selected?
options: It turns into a T cell
interactive_questions.explanation: Once a B cell binds to its specific antigen, it undergoes Clonal Expansion, creating an army of identical cells to fight that specific pathogen. Some become Plasma Cells (fighters), others Memory Cells.

theory.title: Clonal Selection Theory
theory.content:
Your body generates millions of random B cells, each with a unique receptor. When an antigen enters, it will only bind to the B cell with the matching receptor.

This binding event 'selects' that specific B cell to wake up and divide rapidly (clone itself). This ensures resources are only spent making the specific antibodies needed for the current threat.
theory.analogy: Cinderella's Slipper. The Prince (Antigen) travels the kingdom trying the glass slipper on everyone. Only when he finds the one girl it fits (Matching B Cell) does the wedding (Immune Response) happen. He doesn't marry the whole village.
theory.application: This explains why it takes time to fight a new infection (Primary Response)—the body is literally searching through its library of cells to find the one matching book.
